content.title: Response to Reviewer QFpb
content.comment:
Hi, thanks for your comments!

Our paper differs from REALM in terms of motivation and methodology. 

For motivation, REALM mainly equips the model with retrieved knowledge to solve open-domain QA tasks. Our method, as discussed in Section 4, doesn’t equip knowledge to solve those knowledge-intensive tasks, but tries to decouple the intrinsic knowledge already stored in the model parameters and leverage it in an explainable manner (replace FFN where the knowledge is stored). So the problem we try to solve is different from REALM.

For methodology, we use the standard practice, Maximum Inner Product Search, to conduct deep retrieval, which is the same as REALM, kNN-LM, etc. The key insight here is to transform the architecture of FFN to the form of deep retrieval, which has never been done before and it is well grounded in that FFN in transformer is essentially an unnormalized key-value memory network. With that being said, the training objective of our model differs from REALM and our architecture is orthogonal to REALM. For example, we could easily combine REALM into our model by appending the retrieved document to the input, switching FFN in REALM to DPM, and using the concatenated input as the query to our DPM. 

For more details, our model is more lightweight. The REALM model has two components, one BERT-base as the reader, and another BERT-base as a retriever to encode query and document, while our model only adopts attentive pooling of embedding layer as a retriever, which is much faster than REALM as shown in Table1. And because of the quadratic complexity of Self-Attention, the REALM model with concatenated input is also much slower than our model in training and inference.

The only common point of PlugLM and kNN-LM is that we both use MIPS to conduct deep retrieval. The motivation of kNN-LM is to enhance a generative language model with a similar context at the embedding level in the model output layer, while PlugLM tries to decouple the knowledge in the architecture of FFN. These two methods are orthogonal.

Thanks again for your kind suggestion to include a more detailed comparison with those retrieval-augmented PLM, we would append this in the final version of our paper.

We will be happy to address any additional concerns that you might have, and we look forward to engaging in further discussions on our paper.

content.title: Response to Reviewer NzhP
content.comment:
Hi, thanks for the comments. 

As shown in Table 2 and Table 13 in Appendix F, the retrieved knowledge is related to the question-answering pair. (e.g. the definition of United States Census Bureau, knowledge related to states of America). We believe the prerequisite for solving this question-answering NLI problem is to first understand the semantics of Q and A, so PlugLM retrieves relevant pieces of knowledge, which are not unnamed vectors as FFN does, to get a better understanding of Q and A. To fully solve this problem by classifying the relationship between Q and A, we think the role of Self-Attention could not be ignored considering that it captures the contextual interaction among inputs. A joint analysis of DPM and Self-Attention is an interesting problem and we leave this for future exploration.

We hope this could solve your concerns and we will be happy to address any additional concerns that you might have.

content.title: Response to Yury Zemlyanskiy
content.comment:
Thanks so much for pointing out the missing references. We have added these to the related works. Actually, differentiable memory has long been studied[1][2], whether it is in the form of mention, entity, question, or token. The key contribution of our paper is not to design specialized memory to perform a certain knowledge-intensive task, but a general architecture to replace FFN in Transformer with a retrieval mechanism in order to decouple the knowledge otherwise stored in the model parameters, which has never been done before and is orthogonal to all previous methods. Nevertheless, we believe the novel design of better differentiable memory could help us improve the performance of PlugLM.

[1] Graves, Alex, et al. "Hybrid computing using a neural network with dynamic external memory." Nature 538.7626 (2016): 471-476.

[2] Guu, Kelvin, et al. "Retrieval augmented language model pre-training." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2020.

content.title: Response to QFpb
content.comment:
Thanks for your valuable feedback on our paper! Here are the answers to your questions.

Q: Experimental setting.

A: Our main contribution is to propose a novel knowledge encoding mechanism for PLMs, which decouples the learned knowledge during pre-training from the parameters of the PLMs. This enables the knowledge encoding of PLM more flexible and interpretable. Our experimental settings center around one interesting problem: if we manage to decouple the knowledge from PLM, what could we do with it?  We conduct extensive experiments to show that with this novel architecture, we could easily adapt the model to different domains by switching DPM, alleviate catastrophic forgetting by storing DPM, update the model by enlarging DPM, further enhance the model by injecting in-task knowledge into DPM and unveil the black-box PLM with direct access to the knowledge it actually uses. 

Q: Scalability

A: Very good point. Currently, we have 14M entries in the DPM by cutting Wikipedia into chunks. For a super large knowledge corpus, on the one hand, we could resort to efficient dense search like Faiss; on the other hand, we could conduct knowledge filtering or clustering to reduce the size of DPM. This is the first work to verify the validity of decoupling knowledge from parameters and how to make it more efficient and effective remains a promising exploration direction. How to balance general knowledge and domain knowledge is an interesting problem and we think it depends on the task type. For tasks requiring highly intensive domain knowledge, DAR is recommended. 

Q: Other baselines.

A: For baselines like other retrieval-augmented PLM, you could refer to the second point in our response to Reviewer Ry8F. In a nutshell, our method is orthogonal to kNN-LM, which aims to use linear interpolation to enhance the language model in the final output layer with a similar context. Our method tries to decouple the knowledge from FFN. The common point of PlugLM and kNN-LM is to use MIPS to do deep retrieval which is standard practice. The architecture we propose is a very general one and could be used in any Transformer-based model, including kNN-LM or TRIME-LM.

Q: Writing quality and reproducibility.

A: Another round of proofreading is done. Thanks for pointing out all the typos. We will publish our code and model checkpoints once the paper is accepted.

content.title: Response to Reviewer Ry8F (continued)
content.comment:
Clarity problem: 
- PlugLM adopts the same architecture with BERT-base except that we replace the FFN with DPM in the top-N layers. (N=1 as shown in Appendix B).  
- No in-domain training means that we don’t need to further pre-train our model in the specific domain corpus like DAPT does in [1]. We only need to do: 
    1. pre-train PlugLM in the general domain.
    2. construct domain-specific DPM with the trained knowledge encoder.
    3. fine-tune PlugLM with domain-specific DPM (DAA or DAR) in the downstream task.  
- The REALM model has two components: one BERT-base as reader, another BERT-base as retriever to encode query and document. In our setting, the time cost to perform domain adaptation is to encode all domain-specific corpus. REALM uses BERT-base and PlugLM uses attentive pooling of embedding.
- The details of downstream tasks are listed in the Appendix C, Table 9. For further details, you can refer to [1].

[1] Gururangan, Suchin, et al. "Don’t Stop Pretraining: Adapt Language Models to Domains and Tasks." Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics. 2020.

content.title: Response to Reviewer Ry8F
content.comment:
Appreciate your careful and detailed review of our paper. We would explain your concerns point by point:  

Q: The motivation of our work.

A: Our key motivation is to propose a novel knowledge encoding mechanism for PLMs, which decouples the learned knowledge during pre-training from the parameters of the PLMs. This enables the knowledge encoding of PLM more flexible and interpretable. Inspired by previous works[1][2] that show FFN in Transformer acts like a key-value memory network and it is where PLMs store acquired knowledge during pre-training, we creatively use differentiable plug-in memory (DPM) to replace FFN and conduct knowledge retrieval with Maximum inner-product search in DPM, which is the first work to make such exploration, also acknowledged by Reviewer NzhP. Our experimental settings center around one interesting problem: what could we do with that decoupled knowledge from PLM? We conduct extensive experiments to show that with this novel architecture, we could easily adapt the model to different domains by switching DPM, alleviate catastrophic forgetting by storing DPM, update the model by enlarging DPM, further enhance the model by injecting in-task knowledge into DPM and unveil the black-box PLM with direct access to the knowledge it actually uses. 

Q: The difference between our work and retrieval-augmented PLM.

A: Our paper differs from those retrieval-augmented PLM in terms of motivation and methodology. For motivation, those retrieval-augmented PLMs mainly equip the model with retrieved knowledge to solve certain knowledge-intensive tasks, e.g. REALM for open-domain QA. Our method, as discussed in Section 4, doesn’t “inject” (Maybe equip is more appropriate here, thanks for pointing out) knowledge to solve those knowledge-intensive tasks, but tries to decouple the intrinsic knowledge already stored in the model parameters and leverage it in an explainable manner. So the problem we try to solve is different from those retrieval-augmented PLM. For methodology, we use the standard practice, MIPS, to conduct deep retrieval. The architecture of knowledge retrieval is not the essence of our framework and any other methods (e.g. fusion-in-decoder) is viable. The key insight here is to transform the architecture of FFN to the form of deep retrieval, which has never been done before. With that being said, the training objective of our model differs from those retrieval-augmented PLM and our architecture is orthogonal to those retrieval-augmented PLMs. For example, we could easily combine REALM into our model by appending the retrieved document to the input, switching FFN in REALM to DPM, and using the concatenated input as the query to our DPM.  This is the reason why we don't compete with those retrieval-augmented PLM in knowledge-intensive tasks.

Q: Other PLM as retriever and FID attention.

A: The reason why we do not use a pre-trained LM as a retriever or conduct cross-attention on the un-pooled document representation like FID is to align our computational complexity setting with our baseline model, BERT. As shown in Table 4, we have the same model parameters with BERT including our knowledge encoder (Attentive pooler and the Embedder in Equation 5). If we use another PLM as the retriever, although a larger model would typically produce better sentence representation[3], it would be unfair to directly compare with BERT. Also, theoretically, we could store un-pooled knowledge representation in our DPM and conduct cross attention in the same way as FID, but it would cause linear time complexity in the knowledge attention and linear space complexity in DPM storage. Considering the large size of DPM (14M), we choose the current setting.  We have to admit that the current method is based on the standard deep retrieval. But this is the first work to verify the validity of decoupling knowledge from parameters and how to make it more efficient and effective remains a promising exploration direction.



[1] Geva, Mor, et al. "Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Are Key-Value Memories." Proceedings of the 2021 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. 2021.

[2] Dai, Damai, et al. "Knowledge Neurons in Pretrained Transformers." Proceedings of the 60th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2022.

[3] Gao, Tianyu, Xingcheng Yao, and Danqi Chen. "Simcse: Simple contrastive learning of sentence embeddings." arXiv preprint arXiv:2104.08821  (2021).

content.title: Response to Reviewer NzhP
content.comment:
Thanks for your valuable feedback on our paper! Here are the answers to your questions.

Q: Limited Applicability.

A: The proposed replacement of FFN with DPM in Transformer is a general architecture design and since all current PLMs are based on Transformer, it is applicable to any PLMs including RoBERTa. It is true that DPM requires more inference time as listed in Table 4 and we think the current delay is acceptable (×2.54). We would explore more efficient ways as our future work to make it practical in the real world application (e.g. knowledge clustering to reduce the size of DPM or hierarchical-structured DPM as stated in Section 3.4). 

Clarity: 
- Because Transformer consists of stacks of Transformer blocks, here ‘flexibly’ means we don’t replace FFN in every layer with DPM.  As discussed in previous works[1][2], FFN in different layers of PLM may capture knowledge in different levels, either syntactic, semantic or world knowledge. And the optimal solution in our experiments is to replace FFN in top-N layers of Transformer. You could refer to ablation study for more details. 
- “time to encode knowledge” is the time to compute K and V for each document in the domain knowledge and update the DPM. PlugLM doesn't need any in-domain pre-training, which is a de-facto approach for domain adaptation[3]. PlugLM needs fine-tuning. 
- As you suggested, we have conducted more experiments besides STS-B in Section 3.4. The results are shown below. The general pattern here is consistent with the paper. Knowledge captured by pre-trained Transformer differs across layers and injecting knowledge in different types to DPM remains an interesting problem. All newly added experiments together with more cases about retrieved knowledge would be included in the Appendix. 

[1] Warstadt, Alex, et al. "Investigating BERT's knowledge of language: five analysis methods with NPIs." arXiv preprint arXiv:1909.02597 (2019).

[2] Rogers, Anna, Olga Kovaleva, and Anna Rumshisky. "A primer in bertology: What we know about how bert works." Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics8 (2020): 842-866.

[3] Gururangan, Suchin, et al. "Don’t Stop Pretraining: Adapt Language Models to Domains and Tasks." Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics. 2020.

content.title: related works on pluggable memory for Transformers
content.comment:
To follow up on Reviewer QFpb’s comments, I’d like to point out an earlier body of work that incorporates an attention layer over a trainable and pluggable memory into a Transformer. TOME (https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.06176) has MIPS attention layers over a memory of entity mentions and demonstrates 1) backpropagation into memory and 2) updating memory at test time. QAMA (https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.04581), a follow-up, does the same with a question memory. Even earlier work, Entities as Experts (https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.07202) has a trainable memory of entity embeddings. Memorizing Transformer (https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.08913) has a MIPS attention layer over memorized tokens, and (https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.05758) backpropagates into a token memory during pre-training.

It might be worthwhile to discuss these works for readers to get a full picture of the related literature.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a knowledge augmentation method for masked language model. Specifically, they propose a differentiable plug-in memory (DPM) layer with an editable and scalable key-value memory that encodes the knowledge pieces from a corpus. To show the effectiveness of the proposed method, they conduct experiments on domain adaptation downstream tasks (although I am not clear what these downstream tasks are), adding new knowledge after pre-training and incorporating training samples into DPM through knowledge prompting. Authors have compared their method with REALM and specialized pre-trained LM to demonstrate the effectiveness of plug-in knowledge memory.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**:
1. The motivation of this paper to decouple knowledge from the model parameters and utilize external knowledge in an explainable way is great, which also follows the spirit of many works in retrieval-augmented LM.
2. Three interesting experiment settings are considered in this paper to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

**Weaknesses**:
1. This paper explicitly encode knowledge as key-value memory bank and use the hidden states from self-attn to retrieve relevant knowledge, then adds a knowledge attention layer after the self-attn layer. The knowledge retrieval and attention layer is very similar to previous reader models of retrieval-augmented LM.  The only two differences are that the knowledge encoder is trained together with the rest of the model instead of basing on a pre-trained LM, e.g. BERT, and the key to retrieve knowledge is the hidden states from the self-attn layer. Therefore, I think this paper lacks novelty compared to previous works in retrieval-augmented LM. Although this work connects the knowledge integration with FFN, the knowledge attention layer actually functions similarly as a cross-attention layer. Thus it's worth studying whether previous retrieval method works here: using a pre-trained LM as retriever and perform cross attention on the retrieved knowledge or discussing how this paper differs from previous works methodologically.
2. After reading the discussions in the related work, I am more confused by the last sentence of the related work section: 
> One distinct difference of our work is that we do not try to inject additional knowledge into model, but we managed to decouple the knowledge storage from PLM with an editable and scalable DPM and leverage knowledge in an explainable manner.
What does it mean by "decouple" but not "inject additional knowledge"? From your experiments, I think the main advantage of the proposed method is that you can flexibly inject or replace the knowledge bank.
3. If I understand correctly, the proposed method uses pooling to encode each document into a single vector, which would definitely lose lots of the information. And this can lose to those reader models that directly use attention to the retrieved tokens, e.g. the fusion-in-decoder method.
4. Last but not least, I am confused by the choices of tasks used in the experiments. I am not clear what each downstream task refers to in the main results (Table 1). Also, I am not clear why you didn't compare with previous retrieval-augmented LM on some knowledge intensive tasks, e.g. open-domain QA, which makes the value of the proposed method less convincing.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
There are several places in the model description and experiment sections that are unclear to me, which makes it hard to understand or to reproduce the results:

1. It's not clear to me how the knowledge attention layer and FFN layer are placed. In the ablation study (Section 3.4 (3)), Fuse-PlugLM and ALL-PlugLM are explained, but what does PlugLM --- the proposed method in this paper --- look like? It's not clear to me from 2.2, as you used an "or" in the last sentence of the first paragraph in 2.2. Maybe I have missed something.
2. Authors claim that the proposed method doesn't need in-domain training but at the same time uses fine-tuning on downstream tasks, could you clarify what it means by "no training is needed"?
3. Could you explain more why the avg cost of REALM is much higher than PlugLM?

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This work proposes an approach to decouple the storage of knowledge from the rest of a transformer model, using a differential plug-in memory (DPM). The motivation behind doing this is to allow the memory of the model to be editable and scalable.
The core implementation of the plug-in memory uses the idea that transformer feedforward networks can be viewed as key-value memories. The plug-in memory is then implemented by projecting dense representations of each document and projecting them onto key and value pairs. The dense representation of each document is obtained from a knowledge encoder module, that uses attentive pooling. For performing retrieval, they similarly obtain a query vector and conduct maximum inner product search to retrieve the top-N knowledge indices. These top-N knowledge vectors are then aggregated with an attention layer and incorporated into the model.

The experiments are conducted in different scenarios: domain adaptation, knowledge updating and in-task knowledge learning, to demonstrate the different benefits of the proposed approach. 

For their experiments on domain adaptation, they consider domain adaptive post-training and in-domain pretraining as two variants. They compare with REALM, and find that both REALM and PlugLM perform better than domain adaptive pretraining (DAPT -- Gururangan et al, 2019). Further, they find that direct modification of their memory with different domain-specific knowledge is helpful, and more efficient. Using Plug-LM along with in-domain pretraining is also found to be helpful, compared to standard in-domain pretraining. This is shown by comparable performances in these settings across general (GLUE) and domain-specific (biomedical) NER datasets.

Further, the authors also show that it is possible to update the external memory, by gradually enlarging the plug-in memory during finetuning or by gradually replacing knowledge entities in the memory. Finally, they consider explicit fusion of nearest training examples with their plug-in memory. They try multiple approaches, and find that in-task knowledge is best transferred using prompting.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

- The paper presents experiments designed to test all aspects of their plug-in knowledge framework: adaptation to new domains, ability to edit the memory store, and efficiently updating the plug-in knowledge.
- The improvements over the baselines seem consistent and significant across the board. 
- The approach seems intuitive, and is inspired by a previous observation that feedforward networks can be viewed as key-value memory networks.

Weaknesses:

- The experimental settings are often not clearly described. For eg, it wasn't described in sec 3.1.2 as to how the actual experiment was set up and what it was meant to test. I would suggest improving the clarity of all experimental sections.

- Scalability: I'm not sure how this is scalable with a very large corpus unless one is replacing entities in the plug-in memory. Is the assumption that DAR (domain adaptive replacement) is the de-facto way to use the plug-in memory.

- Other baselines?: There seems to be certainly more work that tries to decouple knowledge from the rest of the model computations, that is not cited in this work. For example, kNN-LM (Khandelwal et al), and TRIME-LM (Zhong et al, 2022). The latter might be too recent, but is the former relevant here? Did the authors consider comparing to these works?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- Writing: The writing of the paper still needs a lot of work. The methods and experiments are not described clearly, and it often takes multiple reads to understand what exactly the experiment is testing and how it is being tested. In addition, the paper has many grammatical errors and many misspellings and typos. I only point out a few of them here:
    - The title of the paper has a misspelling - "Knowledge".
    - "plugable" is misspelt.
    - Many terms are used before they are defined, d_2 is used before it is defined in sec 2.1, KnowEnc is used before defining it.
    - "view the each knowledge"
    - "PRETRACINING"
    - "concret"
    - "Concate"
    - "Wikipeida"
    - "GLEU"

- Reproducibility: Although, there isn't a codebase provided in the submission, the authors document many of the hyperparameters in the appendix, which lends more reproducibility to this work.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper presents strong empirical improvements over the baselines they compare with. The experiments consider many different scenarios, all relevant to the initial claims of their approach.

However, the writing and the clarity of the paper needs plenty of work. This is the main weakness of the paper in my opinion.
Other than that, more in-depth discussion of how this work relates to other relevant work would be helpful.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This work proposes a novel language model architecture, PlugLM, which utilizes the differentiable plug-in memory in the Feed-Forward Network (FFN) position inside the transformer layer.

The proposed method shows a decent performance improvement in the domain adaptation setting.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths

- **Important problem and novel solution;** the problem of continually updating the knowledge of PLM is interesting and sounds important. The idea of replacing the transformer layer’s FFN layers with the Key-Value memory network with knowledge memory with the idea of retrieval is novel and significant.
- **Interesting experimental results;** The experimental results on domain-adaptive settings demonstrate the validity and importance of the idea of using external memory inside the transformer layer. The most interesting finding is that switching from Wikipedia as a knowledge source to a domain-specific corpus improves performance in a domain shift in domain shift setting. In addition, the plugLM costs less time for domain adaptation compared to previous methods since it does not require additional training.

### Weaknesses

- **Lack of clarity in writing;** I found several points hard to understand. I believe the quality of the paper might be improved if the authors clarify such points in a future revision. I list those points in the below sections (Clarity, Quality, Novelty, and Reproducibility).
- **Limited Applicability;** All the experiments are conducted with the BERT-base model. Is it applicable to other powerful PLMs such as RoBERTa? In addition, the method also requires more time for inference than the previous approach due to its MIPS search. This characteristic can limit its application in a real-world problem.

### Suggestions

- Typos

page3: $D_h′$ is the explicit knowledge model ‘uses’ to get current prediction → used

page6: one ‘concret’ example → one concete example
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Clarity

It is easy to understand the main idea proposed in the paper. Experimental settings are also comprehensive and results are explained in detail. However, there are several points that need more clarity:

- In Section 2.2: “in PlugLM, for the basic block of each layer, we can flexibly employ FFN to encode the intrinsic language understanding knowledge or DPM to encode the external knowledge from textual corpus”
→ How is the use of FFN and DPM "flexibly" balanced by the PlugLM? According to what I understand, the authors completely replace an FFN from the specified layer (perhaps the final encode layer described in Section 3.4) with the DPM.
- In Section 3.1.1: What does “time to encode the knowledge” mean in detail? Is it just about time to compute K and V values for each document in the domain knowledge and update the DPM? Does the PlugLM require any additional pre-training or fine-tuning?
- Table 2: There is no detailed mention of Table 2 in the main paper. It is hard to understand how to interpret this example. It seems the retrieved knowledge has only a few relations to the input data. Can you provide more explanations on this example? Otherwise, can you provide more examples at least in the Appendix?
- In Section 3.4: “Take STS-B dataset as an example, the Spearman correlation of WikiBERT, …”
→ Experimental results on FFN and DPM indicate that the use of the DPM only is better than combining FFN and DPN in a single layer. Are there additional experimental results on other datasets to consistently prove this observation?

###  Quality
The quality of this work is good. The entire idea can be easily understood. Most experimental settings and results are plausible and well-support the importance of the proposed method.

### Novelty
The novelty of this work is enough. To my knowledge, it is the first work that replaces the FFN layer in the transformer layer with the idea of document retrieval.

### Reproducibility
I cannot find the reproducibility statement in the main manuscript. The authors do not provide any codes or software to reproduce their results. However, the authors do provide some details on the implementations and experimental setups in the Appendix.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The proposed idea of plug-in memory within PLM has enough impact on the field.

However, there are some points that require more clarification to properly support their claim and idea.

Therefore, I rate this work as a weak acceptance.

content.title: Language model with Plug-in Knowldge Memory
content.TL;DR: we propose a pre-training framework to decouple the knowledge storage from PLM
content.abstract: Large-scale pre-trained language models(PLM) have made impressive results in a wide range of NLP tasks and it has been revealed that one of the key factors to their success is the parameters of these models implicitly learn various types of knowledge in the pre-training corpus. However, encoding knowledge implicitly in the model parameters has two fundamental drawbacks. First, the knowledge is neither editable nor scalable once the model is trained, which is especially problematic in that knowledge is consistently evolving. Second, it lacks interpretability and prevents us from understanding what kind of knowledge PLM needs to solve certain task. In this paper, we introduce PlugLM, a pre-training model with differentiable plug-in memory(DPM). The key intuition behind is to decouple the knowledge storage from model parameters with an editable and scalable key-value memory and leverage knowledge in an explainable manner by knowledge retrieval in the DPM.  We conduct extensive experiments under various settings to justify this design choice. In domain adaptation setting, PlugLM could be easily adapted to different domains with plugable in-domain memory---obtaining 3.95 F1 improvements across four domains, without any in-domain training. PlugLM could also keep absorbing new knowledge after pre-training is done by knowledge updating operation in the DPM without re-training. Finally, we show that by incorporating training samples into DPM with knowledge prompting, PlugLM could further be improved by the instruction of in-task knowledge.
